title: Trump, God, and the Struggle for the Chin State
gist: Myanmar's Christian diaspora in the U.S. Midwest has bankrolled the anti-junta insurgency, especially in the resource-poor Chin state, and stays largely pro-Trump through evangelical/MAGA ties, even as Trump's USAID cuts, refugee-program shutdown, TPS termination and ICE raids strain the remittance and support pipeline sustaining the rebellion.

insights.claim: Between 2002 and 2018 the U.S. resettled more refugees from Myanmar than from any other country, mostly Christians now concentrated in Indiana and Minnesota, whose wages from meat-packing, Walmart distribution centers and sushi shops helped fund the anti-junta uprising.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Diaspora remittances are a key financing channel for Myanmar's resistance; U.S. immigration policy directly affects rebel staying power.

insights.claim: Post-coup diaspora funding increasingly shifted to armed struggle, amplified by COVID-era savings growth and social-media crowdfunding that incentivized fighters to keep producing content to sustain flows.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Crowdfunded insurgencies depend on online attention and donor-country household savings; a tighter diaspora economy means weaker rebel financing.
insights.quote: The bulk of the funding increasingly went toward armed struggle

insights.claim: The Chin state, majority-Christian with few natural resources and among Myanmar's poorest, is especially dependent on diaspora support, which constrains rebels from criticizing Trump.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Resource-poor rebel regions are most vulnerable to diaspora funding shocks, unlike mineral-rich fronts.
insights.quote: If we don’t like Donald Trump, we can’t say that, because the diaspora likes him a lot and we rely on them

insights.claim: With no new refugees entering the U.S. and existing immigrants under pressure, the dynamics that sustained support for Myanmar's insurgency may be coming under strain.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Expect weaker funding for Myanmar's resistance, potentially shifting the military balance toward the junta over time.
insights.locator: But with no new refugees moving

insights.claim: Christians are about 6 percent of Myanmar's population but have driven many of its armed rebellions (Karen 1949, Kachin 1960s, Chin 1988), and the junta's Buddhist nationalism leads it to specifically target churches.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Religious framing of the conflict makes it salient to the U.S. Christian right, a lobbying channel into Washington policy.

insights.claim: Persecution has pushed many Myanmar Christians toward a Christian nationalism aligned with the U.S. right, viewing Trump as a protector of Christianity.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Immigrant voting blocs can remain loyal to a party despite adverse policy when religious identity dominates.
insights.quote: For them, ‘Make America Great Again’ means ‘Making Christianity Great Again.’
insights.locator: This experience has led many Christians

insights.claim: Myanmar's diaspora lobbies via evangelical and MAGA networks and has drawn Republican politicians such as Sen. Todd Young to community events.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Congressional Republicans with diaspora constituencies are potential advocates for Myanmar-related sanctions or aid.
insights.locator: The fundraisers were a great place

themes.theme: Aid cuts shift burden to churches

insights.claim: The 2025 cancellation of most USAID programs overwhelmed the Free Burma Rangers, which has 150 relief teams in Myanmar, briefly making it one of the biggest donors, and led to a spike in hunger and death among refugees.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Private and faith-based groups cannot replace state aid at scale; humanitarian conditions in Myanmar are deteriorating.
insights.quote: We are like a volunteer fire department. We can’t sustain large refugee populations.

insights.claim: Some U.S. evangelical leaders welcome USAID cuts as an opportunity for churches to reclaim a central role in welfare and humanitarian care from government.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Ideological support for state retrenchment within the MAGA base reduces pressure to restore foreign aid.
insights.quote: The welfare state, hospitals, universities were all Christian institutions. Over time, they have been more of a humanist thing—let’s win it back

insights.claim: A judge ended temporary protected status for Myanmar nationals in the U.S., putting around 4,000 people at risk of deportation, while dozens have been caught in ICE raids.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Deportation risk shrinks the earning diaspora base that funds Myanmar's resistance.
insights.locator: In the United States, Trump’s policies

insights.claim: Trump's refugee-program shutdown and visa ban on Myanmar nationals has stranded would-be refugees on the Thailand border.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Border refugee pressure in Thailand is likely to build without a U.S. resettlement outlet.

insights.claim: Diaspora support for Trump has dulled after the crackdown but not disappeared, as perceived Democratic hostility to Christian morality keeps many preferring him to the alternative.
insights.speaker: Michael Haack
insights.so_what: Culture-war issues can outweigh direct policy harm in determining immigrant voting behavior.
insights.quote: Though support for the president has dulled among the diaspora, it has hardly gone away.
